messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 47
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Criticised: Being criticised or corrected, Visual (Fire/Flames): Fire or flames, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi was forty-seven years old, a park ranger in a sprawling national forest on the East Coast, and he had not spoken to his sister in eleven months. He had not answered a single call from any of his old friends in two years. He lived alone in a small cabin at the edge of the ranger station’s jurisdiction, and he had come to believe that this was exactly what he deserved. The guilt was not a passing feeling; it was a settled fact, as solid and permanent as the granite outcrops he walked past on his patrols. He had survived, and others had not, and that had to mean something about him—something that made him unfit for the company of people who had not seen what he had seen.

The event that had shattered his life happened fifteen years ago, in a different country, in a different version of himself. Kofi had been a civilian logistics coordinator for a humanitarian aid organization operating in a region that had collapsed into civil war. He was not a soldier, not a combatant, but when the militia overran the town where his team was stationed, there was no distinction. He had hidden in a drainage ditch for seventeen hours while the buildings around him burned. He had watched flames climb the walls of the school where he had delivered food supplies the week before. He had listened to the shouting and the gunfire, and he had stayed still. He had stayed so still that his legs cramped and his jaw ached from clenching. When it was over, he crawled out and walked through the wreckage. He found the bodies of two colleagues who had tried to run. He had not run. He had survived. And he had never been able to make sense of why that calculation—stay still, do not move, do not breathe—had been the right one for him and the wrong one for them.

In the years that followed, he immigrated to the United States and built a quiet life. He became a park ranger because he thought the solitude would heal him. Instead, the solitude became a prison he chose every day. The forest was supposed to be different from that dry, burning town, but it was not. The smell of pine smoke from a distant campfire could stop him cold, his heart hammering as his eyes scanned the treeline for flames that were not there. A sudden shift in the wind through the leaves could sound, to his ears, exactly like the crackle of a roof catching fire. He had come to dread the summer fire season with a visceral terror that his colleagues mistook for professional caution. They corrected him sometimes—on protocol, on trail markings, on the proper way to handle a visitor complaint—and each correction landed like a blow. Being criticised or corrected did not make him angry; it made him feel exposed, as if the person offering the feedback could see right through him to the coward he was certain he still was. He would nod, walk away, and spend the rest of the shift replaying the exchange, convinced that he had been found out.

The avoidance had taken over his life gradually, then completely. He stopped visiting the local bar where the other rangers gathered. He stopped answering his phone. He stopped replying to emails. His sister had flown out to see him twice, and both times he had pretended not to be home, standing still inside his cabin while she knocked, his breath held, until she left. He was certain that if anyone got close enough to know him, they would eventually see the truth: that he had done something wrong, that he had acted against his own values by staying hidden while others died. He had not been brave. He had not been noble. He had been a man in a ditch, and he could not reconcile that with the person he had believed himself to be.

Sleep was a battleground. He lay awake for hours every night, his mind replaying the sound of the flames, the shouting, the silence afterward. When he did drift off, he woke drenched in sweat, disoriented, unsure for a terrible moment whether he was in his cabin or back in that ditch. Even on his days off, when he knew he was safe, he could not relax. His body remained taut, his shoulders hunched, his jaw tight, as if he were still waiting for the militia to find him. And he had developed a strange, exhausting vigilance around time: if a delivery was late, if a hiker did not check in on schedule, if a meeting ran long, his mind immediately jumped to catastrophe. Something bad was happening. He was sure of it. The world had taught him that safety was an illusion, and his brain had learned the lesson too well.

What finally brought him to seek help was not an insight or a crisis, but a small, practical failure. He had been asked to lead a guided hike for a group of visiting schoolchildren, and he had refused. He had said he was busy, but his supervisor had seen through it. The supervisor had sat him down and told him, gently, that his isolation was becoming a problem for the team. Kofi had sat in that meeting and felt the familiar shame rising, the certainty that he was about to be exposed. But his supervisor had not accused him of anything. She had simply asked if he was okay. That question—so ordinary, so kind—had undone him. He had made an appointment with a therapist the next day. He did not know what he was hoping for. He did not believe he deserved to feel better. But he was tired of living in a world where every correction felt like an accusation, every fire a return to that night, and every quiet moment a reminder that he was alone.
